newsitem.title: SPAIN: Arafat to meet Spanish leaders on Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Arafat to meet Spanish leaders on Thursday.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat is to meet Spanish King Juan Carlos and Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar in Madrid on Thursday to commemorate the fifth anniversary of the Middle East peace conference there.
Spain issued separate invitations to Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to come "on or around" October 31, the anniversary of the historic 1991 meeting.
Netanyahu has yet to say whether he will travel to Madrid, and if so when.
Diplomats in Madrid saw Spain's initiative as part of a European effort to reassert itself in a peace process faltering since the hardline Netanyahu won power in Israel in late May.

Last month's outburst of Israeli-Palestinian violence after the opening of an archaeological tunnel in Jerusalem, and now a stalemate over the future of Hebron, has raised tensions to a point at which many now believe the whole process is in peril.
In Luxembourg on Monday, the European Union named Spanish diplomat Miguel Angel Moratinos to be its special envoy to the Middle East.

Diplomats said Moratinos, current ambassador to Israel, had been given a mandate to observe the peace process, establish relations with Israeli and Palestinian negotiators and to report on possible EU actions.

Yasser Arafat began a European tour on Monday in Norway, dismissing U.S. accusations that he was stalling after negotiators had failed to agree on a partial Israeli troop withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron.
He is to meet Irish leaders during a two-day visit to Ireland -- the current EU president -- on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Then, according to Aznar's office, the Palestinian president is to fly on to Madrid on Wednesday evening in time to attend a dinner hosted by Foreign Minister Abel Matutes.
On Thursday the Palestinian leader holds talks with Aznar, give a news conference and then meet the king. He is expected to leave Spain on Friday.

Spanish officials said they had invited Arafat and Netanyahu to Madrid to show their concern for the peace process, but they insisted they had had no intention of trying to bring the t wo men together at a multilateral meeting.
No ceremonies have been planned to mark the landmark conference that brought Israel, Syria, Jordan and Palestinians to the negotiating table after more than four decades of war.
